summary: The text introduces Chart-to-Text, a benchmark for chart summarization aiming to generate natural language summaries from charts to help infer key insights more easily. It includes two datasets with 44,096 charts, highlighting the struggles of state-of-the-art neural models in generating accurate summaries. The text emphasizes the benefits of automatic chart summarization, the challenges faced in interpreting charts, and the need for large-scale benchmarks to advance chart summarization tasks. Various models, including BART and T5, are discussed for text summarization, with a focus on improving generality and insightfulness in the generated summaries. The text discusses the importance of providing alternative text for visualizations to assist individuals with visual impairments in understanding complex data. It emphasizes the need to reference underlying data instead of visual elements to reduce cognitive burden and provides recommendations for composing informative alternative texts. The study highlights the benefits of visualizations in summarizing data effectively and the potential for assistive technologies to bridge the gap for individuals with visual impairments. The text also discusses challenges in integrating tactile visualizations and data sonification into online environments and the importance of using text to convey information in visualizations, especially in web environments. The text compares the effectiveness of Free Response Image Description (FRID) and Queried Image Description (QID) methods for creating image descriptions for individuals with visual impairments, particularly in the STEM field. The study found that QID descriptions were more comprehensive and standardized, with fewer omissions and more consistency among describers. The research emphasizes the importance of providing information about images to novice web workers using templates and guidelines, as well as the potential for automated systems to generate image summaries. Future research is recommended to further enhance the quality and usability of image descriptions for individuals with visual impairments.

The text introduces a new dataset and neural model for generating natural language summaries of charts, aimed at aiding visually impaired individuals and those with low visualization literacy. The model, based on a transformer architecture, outperforms existing models in content selection and generates informative, concise, and coherent summaries of key insights from charts. The study highlights the importance of chart summarization for various user groups, discusses limitations of existing methods, and proposes a new approach to address challenges such as data hallucination and inaccurate predictions. The model's performance is evaluated through human assessments and comparisons with baseline models, showing improvements in informativeness, conciseness, coherence, and factual correctness. The authors aim to inspire further research in this under-explored area and plan to expand their dataset

The text discusses the development of DataShot, an automated system that generates fact sheets from tabular data by extracting data facts, organizing them into topics, and mapping them to visualizations. The system aims to streamline the process of creating visually appealing fact sheets by automatically generating them based on common infographic design structures and styles. The research validates the effectiveness of DataShot through real-world datasets and an in-lab user study, demonstrating its ability to simplify the creation of fact sheets and make data more understandable and visually appealing for general users.

The article discusses the development of a course on Audio Description at the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, focusing on the competences and skills required for future professionals in the field. It emphasizes the importance of audio describers being social intermediaries who make audiovisual material accessible to those with sensory difficulties, and highlights the necessary competences such as linguistic abilities, cultural understanding, and technical skills. The course includes exercises on describing physical objects, analyzing visuals, and creating audio descriptions for film clips to develop students' skills in audio description. The text also discusses the challenges, importance, and future prospects of audio description in the field of media accessibility.

The text discusses the importance of inclusive data visualization for individuals with disabilities, highlighting the challenges faced by those with visual, cognitive, and motor impairments in accessing visual data. It emphasizes the need for collaboration between visualization practitioners, accessibility researchers, and disability communities to prioritize accessibility in data visualization. The text explores various methods for making visual data accessible, such as alt text, sonification, tactile graphics, and touchscreen-based presentations, and calls for more research in this area. It also addresses ethical and structural challenges in conducting research with populations with different abilities, emphasizing the importance of developing new visualization and interaction idioms to cater to diverse abilities and contexts. The text explores the integration of text and visualizations in interactive web documents, proposing a framework that allows for details on demand, visual highlighting, comparison, and brushing-and-linking. It introduces the concept of sparklines to embed visualizations within text and discusses the use of CSS style sheets to manage the appearance of interactive elements. The framework aims to link text to visualizations through markups, allowing for interactive entities to be defined declaratively. The text also discusses the importance of data and visualizations in creating interactive documents, highlighting the dynamic generation of legends and the use of triggers for user interactions. Additionally, the text outlines potential future research directions and acknowledges financial support for the project.

The text discusses the GeoExplainer visual analytics framework, which supports spatial modeling, contextualization, and reporting through interactive views and template-based narrative generation. The framework aims to explain statistical indicators, interpret spatial patterns, and enhance communication of spatial models. It includes features such as model configuration, validation, narrative generation, report authoring, and analytical state recording. The text also highlights the usability evaluation of the framework, expert interviews, and the development of a narrative generation pipeline. Additionally, the text references various research papers and tools related to spatial analysis, visualization, geographically weighted regression, and machine learning in the context of spatial data analysis.

The text discusses a research paper on accessible visualization through natural language descriptions, focusing on a four-level model of semantic content. The paper includes a multi-line chart illustrating the impact of controlling the transmission of COVID-19 on the number of cases, highlighting the importance of communication to the public about the potential outcomes of the crisis. The paper was received in March 2021, revised in June 2021, and accepted in August 2021, with a publication date of September 2021. The research explores the effectiveness of visualization descriptions for different reader groups, emphasizing the importance of conveying trends and statistics in a reader-specific manner. The study explores the use of neural methods for generating captions for line charts, developing a model that outperforms non-neural baselines and shows potential for data-driven captioning of time-series visualizations. The research involves creating a dataset through crowdsourcing, training an encoder-decoder architecture on human-labeled datasets, and comparing different models for text generation. Experimental results indicate that the neural model is superior in generating captions, with plans for future research including error analysis, larger dataset collection, and exploring more sophisticated input representations. The study references various related research papers and systems in the fields of natural language processing, visualization design, and computational linguistics.

VoxLens is an open-source JavaScript plug-in developed by researchers at the University of Washington to improve the accessibility of online data visualizations for screen-reader users. The plug-in offers voice-activated commands, sonified data playback, and three modes of interaction to help users extract information more accurately and efficiently. Task-based experiments showed significant improvements in information extraction accuracy and interaction time compared to conventional methods, with users describing VoxLens as a valuable tool for making online data visualizations more accessible. The tool is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution International 4.0 License and will be presented at CHI '22 in New Orleans.

The text explores the emerging trend of narrative visualization in journalism and educational media, discussing design strategies, storytelling techniques, and the balance between author-driven and reader-driven elements. It highlights the importance of interactivity, messaging, and visual elements in conveying narratives effectively. The text also discusses the use of visualizations in various topics, including sports statistics, economic data, and global issues, showcasing examples of successful narrative visualizations and suggesting areas for further research and development in the field.

The text discusses the challenges faced by screen-reader users when accessing online data visualizations, highlighting their struggles to extract information accurately and efficiently. Screen-reader users often find visualizations to be inaccessible and incomprehensible, leading to inequalities in accessing essential information. The study suggests that tabular and textual representations of data could improve accessibility for screen-reader users, emphasizing the need for more accessible design in online visualizations. Additionally, the text explores the experiences of screen-reader users, the impact of different visualization libraries, and the importance of alternative text and ARIA attributes in improving accessibility for this user group.

The Eurographics Conference on Visualization (EuroVis) 2022 featured a paper by Zong et al. from MIT, Carnegie Mellon, and UCL on improving accessibility for data visualization through rich screen reader experiences. The paper identifies limitations of current non-visual alternatives for screen readers and proposes a new approach allowing for interactive data exploration at different levels of granularity. Through a co-design process, the authors identify three key design dimensions for expressive screen reader accessibility: structure, navigation, and description. The study highlights the challenges faced by screen reader users when interacting with visualizations and the importance of providing rich and usable screen reader experiences for web-based visualizations. The text explores the preferences of blind and low vision individuals for image descriptions in various digital contexts, emphasizing the importance of nuanced descriptions and the lack of alt text for accessibility. Findings show that preferences vary based on the source of the images, with recommendations provided for the development of more accessible image description technologies. The study conducted qualitative research with 28 participants to understand their experiences and preferences with digital images on different sources, such as news websites, social networking sites, and e-publications. Participants expressed frustration with inadequate image descriptions on various platforms and emphasized the need for more detailed descriptions to enhance accessibility. The text also discusses the limitations of current AI systems in generating accurate descriptions and suggests personalized approaches for providing image descriptions based on individual preferences. The text explores the challenges faced by blind and visually impaired users in accessing social media content with embedded imagery, focusing on the limitations of AI image captioning systems and the potential of conversational crowdsourcing to improve accessibility. The study highlights the importance of human-in-the-loop workflows, structured question and answer approaches, and personalized alt text to enhance the understanding of images for visually impaired individuals. The research emphasizes the need for scalable, cost-effective solutions that balance automation with human input to provide accurate and valuable image descriptions for blind users on social media platforms like Twitter.

The text discusses the need for an automatic evaluation method for machine translation that is quick, language-independent, and highly correlated with human evaluation. It proposes a method based on n-gram matches and modified precision scores to rank candidate translations against reference translations. The text highlights the importance of selecting appropriate word choices, enforcing proper translation length, and calculating brevity penalties in evaluation. It also explores the use of the BLEU metric to predict bilingual judgments and accelerate research in machine translation. The study compares different systems and human translators, emphasizing the limitations of automated translation compared to human proficiency. The text concludes that BLEU is effective in distinguishing between translations of varying quality and can help researchers identify effective modeling ideas for machine translation.

The text discusses the integration of interactive data facts into visualization tools like Voder to aid in data exploration and communication. Users can search for specific data facts, explore alternative visualizations, and customize their findings through interactive widgets. A user study with 12 participants showed that interactive data facts helped users interpret visualizations and explore alternative ways to communicate their findings. The text highlights the importance of trust in NLG-based systems and suggests future research directions for enhancing user interactions with visualizations.

The text discusses a study on how different visual arrangements of bar charts can impact viewer comparisons and takeaways. Participants were asked to identify patterns and comparisons in various chart arrangements, with findings suggesting that well-designed visualizations can lead to more intuitive processing. The study categorized viewer takeaways based on visual arrangements, established a taxonomy for visual comparisons, and compared results with expert intuitions. Recommendations were made for visualization designers to consider spatial arrangements to facilitate key comparisons among data values. The text also highlights the importance of exploring visual affordances for conjunction comparisons and improving natural language interfaces for mapping verbal takeaways to visual comparisons. Future research areas include investigating the impact of visualization arrangements on comparison accuracy and exploring techniques to help designers choose the best arrangement for accurate data interpretation.

The text explores the k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) algorithm, a simple yet effective machine learning technique used for classification and regression. It discusses the concept of KNN, its applications in various fields such as healthcare and stock market forecasting, and the importance of selecting the appropriate value of K for optimal results. The text also mentions improvements and variations of the algorithm, including locally adaptive KNN, weight adjusted KNN, and KNN combined with SVM. Additionally, it touches on the significance of data analysis, data mining, and advancements in artificial intelligence for enhancing the speed and accuracy of KNN classifiers in machine learning algorithms.

The text discusses the development of Chart Reader, a web-based accessibility engine that enables blind and low vision individuals to access and understand visualizations through a co-design process involving 10 design partners. The tool incorporates non-speech audio, navigation options, and sonification features to enhance the accessibility of data visualizations. The study highlights the importance of providing varied access points to information, customizable options, and hierarchical structures to manage the complexity of charts for visually impaired users. Lessons learned from the co-design study aim to improve the creation of accessible visualization experiences for other chart types and emphasize the importance of multiple communication methods in data visualization.

The text introduces a new Transformer-based model for data-to-text generation that improves content correctness and performance by modifying the latent representation of the input and incorporating an additional learning objective for content selection modeling. Two data augmentation methods are proposed to enhance the model's performance, leading to better results in terms of BLEU, content selection precision, and content ordering compared to existing systems. The model has been publicly released for use and addresses challenges in content selection and text generation in data-to-text tasks.

The text explores the concept of visualization rhetoric in narrative visualizations, discussing how design techniques can influence user interpretation and the importance of understanding rhetorical techniques in visualization design. It highlights the impact of bias, framing, and perspective on interpretation, as well as the role of semiotics and rhetorical strategies in shaping user perceptions. The text emphasizes the need for transparency, data provenance, and the consideration of individual and cultural viewing codes in visualization design. It also discusses the potential for future research in understanding and applying visualization rhetoric to improve the effectiveness and clarity of visual representations.

The text discusses a study on domain scientists' trust in visual analytics systems compared to conventional analysis methods, focusing on the usability and efficiency of the Active Data Biology tool. The study found that participants had a high level of trust in visual analytic tools that were intuitive, transparent, and allowed for seamless switching between hypothesis generation and evidence gathering. The study also showed that visual analytic systems were trusted more than manual data analysis methods for complex tasks, regardless of participants' experience and familiarity. The text highlights the importance of understanding trust in visual analytics systems and the need for further research to improve the design of future tools for domain scientists.

The text introduces ChartReader, a unified framework that integrates chart derendering and comprehension tasks without heuristic rules or OCR systems. By automatically learning chart rules from annotated datasets, ChartReader reduces manual effort and improves accuracy. The framework includes a transformer-based chart component detection module and a pre-trained vision-language model for various tasks like chart-to-table and ChartQA. Evaluation shows ChartReader's superiority over existing methods, offering a significant reduction in manual effort for chart analysis and moving towards a universal chart understanding model.

The text discusses the importance of low-level analysis tasks in information visualization to understand user behavior and facilitate analytic activity. It presents a set of ten tasks based on sample questions collected from students analyzing data sets, serving as a common substrate for system designers to discuss capabilities and evaluate systems. The text also explores taxonomies of system tasks, the shift towards "analytic primacy," and the development of a Data State Reference Model. It discusses various data analysis tasks, challenges in creating taxonomies, and the limitations of tools for thought and evaluation in data analysis. The text emphasizes the need for innovative visualization techniques, the importance of analytic measures, and the role of primitive analysis task types in assessing new systems. The text introduces the problem of figure caption generation and proposes a novel attention mechanism to automatically generate natural language descriptions for figures. The authors introduce the FigCAP dataset and train the captioning model using reinforcement learning to address exposure bias, outperforming baselines in experiments. The text discusses the importance of attention mechanisms, reinforcement learning, and hybrid training objectives in generating high-quality captions for figures, with potential applications in improving user experience for visually impaired individuals and parsing large amounts of figures in PDF documents.

The text discusses the importance of visualization literacy (VL) and outlines a method for assessing users' abilities to interpret visual information effectively through tests for line graphs, bar charts, and scatterplots using Item Response Theory. The study involves calibrating and validating the tests on MTurk, with results showing that the tests are effective for differentiating examinees with low abilities. The text emphasizes the need for fast and reliable tests to detect low-ability participants in online studies and provides guidelines for designing and analyzing test items to ensure accuracy in assessing visualization literacy levels.
